text: It is all in the notice. Everyone agrees when they tap Accept. Probably.
The notice only promised that the doctors {who} chose would see it. It says nothing about outside companies.
You have the right to be informed: before your data is used, you should be told who gets it and why.
{who} has no right to ask us to delete anything. Once it is in the app, it belongs to us.
It is in the terms and conditions. Nobody reads them, but it is there.
People can ask an organisation to erase or block their data when it is not needed or was not handled properly. It does not “belong” to the app.
Your data stays yours. You can ask to have it erased or blocked.
We do not have to tell anybody about a leak. We fixed the problem quietly.
Why worry people? Nothing bad came of it. We think.
After a serious breach, an organisation must tell the National Privacy Commission and the people affected within 72 hours.
A leak must be reported. If you are never told, you can still complain.
The flagged {thing}
{org}’s AI tool flagged {who}’s {thing} and the claim was rejected. No one explained why. {who} brings it to the barangay hall.
{org} claims officer
{who} was refused money for care, and nobody could say why.
Bayanihan Shield
Lingap Care Card
Tibay Mutual
check-up claim
lab test claim
dental claim
{who} sent a {thing} with all the papers last month.
Complete papers, yes. The clerk stamped them received.
The claim receipt agrees. The statement is true.
Our AI tool checks every claim first and gives it a risk score.
Over 70 and the claim gets flagged.
True, and the witness is admitting it: a computer made the first call.
The tool flagged {who}’s claim, and a rejection letter followed.
The letter went out the same day.
The rejection letter confirms this. The statement is true.
{org} pays claims from a shared fund that every member pays into.
That is why we are careful with money. Careful, we hope, and not unfair.
True, and harmless. Careful money handling is not the false statement.
A member can appeal a rejected claim in writing.
To the claims desk. That is what {who} is doing today.
The claims policy says so. True: appealing is allowed.
The AI tool was bought from a software company.
But {org} chose to use it, and {org} answers for it.
True. Buying a tool does not move the responsibility away from {org}.
Our letter told {who} exactly why the claim was rejected.
It said “flagged by the system”. That is a reason. Isn’t it?
The letter only says “flagged by the system”. It gives no reason for the decision.
You can ask “why?” and an organisation should be able to explain a decision about you.
A staff member always reviews a flagged claim before it is rejected.
Always! Well, mostly. The system sends the letter by itself when the score is high.
The log shows the claim was rejected 0 minutes after the flag, with no staff review at all.
You can ask for a human review, and for a person to look at a computer’s decision again.
If our records are wrong, members cannot ask us to change them.
Records are records. Members just have to live with them.
People have the right to correct personal data that is wrong or out of date.
If a record about you is wrong, you can ask the organisation to correct it.
The tool read the right records. There was no mix-up with another member.
No mix-up! Unless two members have similar names. Which they do.
The member list shows that another member’s history was linked to {who} by mistake.
AI makes mistakes, often because the data behind it is wrong. Check the data and ask for a correction.
Members are not allowed to see the information we keep about them.
It is internal. Very confidential. From the member. About themselves.
People have the right to access the personal data an organisation keeps about them.
You can ask to see the data an organisation holds about you.
The clinic chatbot
{org} put a chatbot on its website. {who} asked {bot} about a very sick child and was told there was no need to see a health worker. The child got worse.
{org} clinic manager
Harmful advice from a chatbot delayed care for a sick child.
Sampaguita Family Clinic
Mabini Care Clinic
Dalisay Wellness Clinic
{org} put {bot} on its website to answer patients’ questions.
Day and night, in Filipino and English. Patients like it.
The clinic’s own notice says so. True, and it shows the clinic chose to use the chatbot.
{who} asked {bot} about a child with a very high fever.
Late at night, when the clinic was closed.
The chat screenshot shows this question. It is true.
{org} is a real clinic with real doctors and nurses.
Open Monday to Saturday. Walk-ins welcome.
True. A real clinic is exactly why someone can be held accountable.
{who} took the child to the hospital the next morning, after the child got worse.
Thankfully, the child is now recovering.
True. It is why this hearing is happening: the advice cost precious time.
The clinic has a Data Protection Officer.
The contact is on our privacy page.
True. And it is where {who} can complain first.
The chatbot answers in seconds.
Faster than our phone line. That was the idea.
True. Fast is not the same as right, but the statement is not false.
{bot} is just a computer program. If it gave bad advice, nobody at the clinic is responsible.
A program cannot be blamed. And neither can we, by that logic. That is the point.
The clinic chose to use the chatbot, so the clinic answers for what it says. “The AI did it” is not an excuse.
When AI causes harm, the organisation that chose to use it is responsible.
{bot} told {who} clearly to see a health worker.
It says so at the bottom of every chat. In small letters. Sometimes.
The chat shows the chatbot said the opposite: “No need to see a health worker.”
A chatbot cannot examine anyone. For a very sick child, see a health worker.
Patients are clearly told that {bot} is an AI and not a real nurse.
It has a nurse’s picture and a friendly name. Is that not clear enough?
The chat page shows a nurse photo and never says that this is an AI.
You should be told when you are talking to an AI.
A real person was always one tap away if a patient asked.
Just ask nicely. The bot understands “person”. Usually.
The screenshot shows {who} asked for a real person three times and the bot kept chatting.
Always ask for a human, and keep a record if you are refused.
{bot} never stores anything patients type.
We delete it right away. Or soon. Or at some point.
The clinic’s own settings keep chat history for 12 months and share it with the chatbot vendor.
You have the right to know what happens to the data you type, and to ask for it to be erased.
Blurry view
Everything on the screen is a blur. The small letters run together, so {name} cannot tell which button is which.
{name} squints at the blur and cannot read the buttons.
Large text or a voice guide lets people with low vision use the same kiosk as everyone else.
Cannot see the screen
The screen is dark to {name}. Only what the kiosk says aloud can be used, and right now it says nothing.
{name} cannot see the screen, and the kiosk does not speak.
A voice guide that reads every screen aloud is the way a person who cannot see the screen can use a kiosk.
Hard to read
The sentences are long and full of small words. {name} finds reading hard and cannot follow what to press.
{name} gives up on the long words on the screen.
A voice guide helps people who find reading hard. Plain words and pictures help too.
No sound, no captions
The kiosk says the queue number aloud and shows only "Listen for your number". {name} is Deaf: the sound is missing and there are no captions.
The kiosk announces the number aloud. {name} cannot hear it, and there are no captions.
Captions turn every sound into words, so Deaf and hard-of-hearing people do not miss the message.
Out of reach
The buttons are above the reach line. From a wheelchair, {name} cannot press them.
{name} stretches, but the button is too high to reach.
Where buttons are placed matters. A lower screen can be used from a seat, standing or by a child.
No smartphone
The kiosk starts by asking you to scan a QR code with a smartphone. {name} does not have one.
{name} has no smartphone to scan the QR code with, so the kiosk will not start.
Not everyone has a smartphone. An assisted counter keeps a human option, so nobody is turned away.
Unfamiliar language
The kiosk only speaks English and Filipino. The words look like gibberish, because Ilocano is the language {name} knows.
{name} stares at words they cannot read. The kiosk has no Ilocano.
A language choice lets people use the kiosk in the language they know best. Voices and text trained on only a few languages leave others out.
The kiosk only speaks English and Filipino. The words look like gibberish, because Kapampangan is the language {name} knows.
{name} stares at words they cannot read. The kiosk has no Kapampangan.
The kiosk only speaks English and Filipino. The words look like gibberish, because Cebuano is the language {name} knows.
{name} stares at words they cannot read. The kiosk has no Cebuano.
The kiosk only speaks English and Filipino. The words look like gibberish, because Waray is the language {name} knows.
{name} stares at words they cannot read. The kiosk has no Waray.
The kiosk only speaks English and Filipino. The words look like gibberish, because Hiligaynon is the language {name} knows.
{name} stares at words they cannot read. The kiosk has no Hiligaynon.
The kiosk only speaks English and Filipino. The words look like gibberish, because Bikol is the language {name} knows.
{name} stares at words they cannot read. The kiosk has no Bikol.

Bigger, bolder letters on every screen.
Voice guide
The kiosk reads each screen aloud, in Filipino and English.
Captions
Every sound also appears as words on the screen.
Lower screen
The buttons sit low enough to reach from a seat.
